questions.stem: A 75-year-old man was admitted from his nursing home with several days of fever, nonproductive cough, headache, and diarrhea. The nursing staff mentioned that two other patients had also been unwell and had had fevers and respiratory symptoms. On admission, the patient had a temperature of 38.5°C, pulse of 110 beats/minute, blood pressure 98/50 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 89% on room air. His initial laboratory evaluation was notable for a sodium of 125, creatinine of 1.6, and white blood cell count of 16,000. Chest radiograph showed bilateral, diffuse, interstitial, pulmonary opacities. Cultures were ordered, and broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated.
questions.lead_in: Of the listed antibacterials, which of the following would be most likely to be effective against the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin This patient is presenting with a syndrome compatible with atypical pneumonia. It is also noteworthy that there was a cluster of sick patients at his nursing home, which could be suggestive of a spreading respiratory viral infection or Legionella, which has been associated with hospital and nursing home-related outbreaks because of contaminated water sources. Hyponatremia, acute renal failure, abnormal liver function tests, and gastrointestinal symptoms may be seen with legionellosis. Other causes of atypical pneumonia can include M. pneumonia and C. pneumonia, which can also be treated with azithromycin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q37

questions.question: Aerosol-transmitted organisms that are not thought to spread person-to-person.

parts.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.

questions.model_answer: (1) Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) - acquired by inhalation of contaminated aerosols; person-to-person spread is negligible, so hospitalized patients need not be isolated unless undergoing an aerosolizing procedure or recently delivered. (2) Coccidioides immitis (or, equally acceptable, Histoplasma capsulatum, Brucella spp., or Legionella pneumophila) - acquired by aerosol inhalation without person-to-person transmission.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only Coxiella is grounded in this chapter; Coccidioides/Histoplasma/Brucella/Legionella are established non-person-to-person aerosol pathogens from general Mandell/CDC knowledge.

questions.question: A 12-year-old with Crohn disease on a TNF-alpha inhibitor returns from an August family vacation with a 3-day history of fever, non-productive cough and diarrhea. Admitted with respiratory distress and a chest x-ray showing multilobar pneumonia, started on piperacillin-tazobactam, then deteriorates and requires PICU admission for hypoxemic respiratory failure.
questions.question_raw: 12 year old patient with Crohns on TNF alpha who came back from vacation with family in august with 3 days history of fever, non productive cough and diarrhea. Admitted for respiratory distress with CXR of multilobar pneumonia. Started on piptazo. Worsened and requires admission to PICU with hypoxemic respiratory failure.

parts.text: What is the likely syndrome?
Name 2 investigations with one advantage and one disadvantage each (Test / Advantage / Disadvantage).

parts_raw.text: What is the likely syndrome

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila pneumonia) - suggested by anti-TNF-alpha immunosuppression, summer travel, non-productive cough with diarrhea, multilobar pneumonia failing to respond to a beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam has no anti-Legionella activity), and progression to respiratory failure.
b) (1) Urine antigen - Advantage: rapid, easy to perform, highly specific (>99%) and often positive early; Disadvantage: detects essentially only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so insensitive for other serogroups/species. (2) Lower respiratory (sputum/endotracheal aspirate) culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract - Advantage: 100% specific, detects all serogroups/species and yields an isolate for outbreak fingerprinting; Disadvantage: requires special media and expertise, and yield is reduced by prior antibiotics.
c) (1) Macrolides - azithromycin, clarithromycin. (2) Fluoroquinolones - levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin. Preferred first-line agents are azithromycin or levofloxacin.

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila pneumonia) - anti-TNF-alpha therapy is a significant risk factor, and maintenance work implies exposure to aerosolized water; multilobar pneumonia failing a beta-lactam with diarrhea and respiratory failure fits.
b) (1) Urine antigen - Advantage: rapid, easy, highly specific and often positive when other tests are negative; Disadvantage: mainly detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 (insensitive for other serogroups/species). (2) Lower respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract - Advantage: 100% specific, detects all species/serogroups and provides an isolate for source investigation; Disadvantage: needs special media/expertise and is insensitive, with yield lowered by prior antibiotics.
c) (1) Macrolides - azithromycin, clarithromycin. (2) Fluoroquinolones - levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin (preferred first-line: azithromycin or levofloxacin). If neither class can be used, an alternative is doxycycline (a tetracycline).

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionella pneumophila - failure of a beta-lactam in severe pneumonia with hyponatremia and elevated liver enzymes is the classic clue.
b) (1) Urine antigen - Advantage: rapid, easy, highly specific (>99%); Disadvantage: detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1. (2) Lower respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract - Advantage: 100% specific and detects all species/serogroups (yields isolate); Disadvantage: requires special media/expertise and is insensitive. c) (1) Azithromycin (macrolide). (2) Levofloxacin (fluoroquinolone). (3) Doxycycline (tetracycline).

questions.question: Two patients in your hospital have acquired Legionella pneumonia. The source is suspected to be the potable water distribution system in your hospital.
questions.question_raw: Two patients in your hospital have acquired Legionella pneumonia. The source is suspected to be the potable water distribution system in your hospital.

parts.text: What are TWO short-term solutions that can be implemented to immediately reduce the risk of infection?
What are THREE long-term solutions to prevent the risk of infection in the future?

parts_raw.text: What are TWO short-term solutions that can be implemented to immediately reduce the risk of infection?
What are THREE long-term solutions to prevent the risk of infection in the future?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Take the implicated potable-water source out of operation and provide sterile/bottled water for drinking and for nasogastric irrigation of high-risk patients. (2) Perform emergency disinfection of the water system per local guidelines (e.g., superheat-and-flush or hyperchlorination).
b) (1) Implement secondary disinfection of the hot-water system (e.g., monochloramine), which reduces Legionella colonization and nosocomial LD. (2) Establish a formal water management program with risk assessment and scheduled monitoring/environmental culturing. (3) Ensure proper building, cooling-tower and plumbing design, construction and ongoing maintenance (with IPC involvement in future construction/renovation).

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila) - anti-TNF-alpha therapy is a recognized risk factor, and pneumonia failing a beta-lactam with hyponatremia is classic.
b) (1) Urine antigen - Limitation: detects essentially only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so a negative test does not exclude other serogroups/species. (2) Lower respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract - Limitation: requires special media and expertise, is insensitive, and yield drops once antibiotics are started.
c) (1) Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin). (2) Fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin).
d) Doxycycline (a tetracycline).

cohort_answer.text: Legionella pneumophila. TNF-alpha inhibitors increase risk of intracellular pathogens (2-4 fold increase in TB and other granulomatous conditions; also Listeria, Legionella, Salmonella, HBV, VZV, JC virus, possible NTM/Nocardia, case reports of Crypto/Histo/Cocci). Tests: Urine legionella antigen (only detects serogroup 1) and culture (needs specialized charcoal-containing media); can also do DFA. Treatment classes: fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin), macrolides (azithromycin). Alternative: doxycycline.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Immediately stop using the potable water linked to the outbreak and supply sterile/bottled water for high-risk patients. (2) Perform emergency disinfection of the water system per local policy (superheat-and-flush or hyperchlorination).
b) (1) Scheduled water testing/environmental surveillance. (2) Scheduled water treatment with secondary disinfection (e.g., monochloramine). (3) A formal water management program with risk assessment and proper engineering/plumbing design and maintenance, with IPC involved in future construction/renovation.

cohort_answer.text: Short term: Immediately stop using potable water linked to the site causing the outbreak; Immediately treat water system as per local policy. Long term: Scheduled water testing; Scheduled water treatments; Ensure IPC involved in all future construction/renovations so that interventions are in place to avoid future outbreaks

questions.question: Recreational water exposure.

parts.text: Give two causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure.
Give one (or two) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure.
What is the most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

parts_raw.text: 2 causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure?
1 (or 2) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure
Most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Pseudomonas aeruginosa hot tub folliculitis (also hot hand-foot syndrome/green nail syndrome). (2) Nontuberculous mycobacteria (Mycobacterium avium complex). b) (1) Mycobacterium avium complex hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'). (2) Legionella pneumophila. c) Cryptosporidium species - the most frequent pathogen implicated in recreational-water outbreaks and a leading parasitic cause of waterborne diarrhea (Giardia is the other principal cause).
questions.beyond_mandell: Hot tub lung (MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis), Legionella, and nontuberculous mycobacterial dermatitis are not in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general/PHAC-CDC waterborne-disease knowledge.
questions.cohort_conflict: The chapter identifies Cryptosporidium as the most frequent recreational-water pathogen, so for waterborne illness Cryptosporidium is favored over the cohort's Giardia.

cohort_answer.text: Dermatitis: Hot tub folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) - painful pruritic pustules within 24-48h, self-resolves 7-14d; Hot foot syndrome (Pseudomonas) - painful red nodular lesions on soles, self-limiting 7-10d; Green nail syndrome (pseudomonas) with onychomycosis; Mycobacterium species. Pneumonia: MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'), usually self-limiting, may need prednisone +/- antimycobacterial; Legionellosis (usually L. pneumophila). Parasite: Giardia lamblia (most common cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide; cryptosporidium also very high incidence); tx metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide, paromomycin if pregnant first trimester
